c.tagline: Whitewashed Casbah alleys tumble to a sweeping Mediterranean bay.

taxi.fareNote: Official taxis are metered with a small starting fare plus per-km charge; agree on a price beforehand for airport or intercity trips, as meters are sometimes 'not working' for tourists.

emergency.note: Gendarmerie Nationale can also be reached at 1055; French is widely understood by responders, English less so.

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing in the Casbah and city centre; caution at night

hood_desc: The historic heart of Algiers around the UNESCO-listed Casbah and Place des Martyrs, with colonial Haussmann-style boulevards, the cheapest lodging, and easy walking access to museums and street food; suits first-time visitors and budget travelers.

An affluent, leafy hillside suburb of embassies, upscale apartments, and restaurants overlooking the bay; suits business travelers and those wanting a quiet, secure base a short taxi ride from downtown.
A cooler hilltop colonial-era quarter of villas and gardens above the city, home to the storied Hotel El Djazair; suits couples and travelers wanting atmosphere and calm away from downtown traffic.
A seafront strip of pine-lined resort and conference hotels east of downtown, anchored by the Hilton and Sheraton Club des Pins; suits business visitors and families wanting a pool or beach access.
A modern business and university district near the airport with international chain hotels and convention facilities; suits transit travelers and conference-goers prioritizing airport proximity.

water.note: Aging pipes mean tap water carries contamination risk; drink bottled water instead.

transit.pay: Metro and tram use paper tickets or rechargeable cards bought at station counters/machines and validated at gates or onboard validators; buses are typically paid in small-denomination cash to the driver or conductor. Contactless bank-card payment is not yet common on public transit.
transit.hours: Metro and tram operate roughly 5:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m.; buses run similar daytime hours with sparse or no late-night service, after which taxis are the main option.
transit.note: Network is limited to one metro line, one tram line, and buses; central Algiers and the Casbah are best explored on foot given steep, narrow streets.

train: SNTF national rail linking Algiers to Oran, Constantine, Annaba and other cities
bus: Intercity coaches from Gare Routière Caroubier
ferry: Algérie Ferries seasonal routes to Marseille and Alicante

transit.m: Airport shuttle/city bus to Grande Poste (~40-50 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up the bill or leaving 5-10% in sit-down restaurants is appreciated but rarely expected, and taxi drivers are not usually tipped.

food.name: Couscous
food.desc: Algeria's national dish: hand-rolled steamed semolina under a broth of lamb, chicken or, on the Algiers coast, fish, with chickpeas and turnip.

places.name: Restaurant El Djenina
places.note: Rue Bab Azoun institution mixing Algerian and French cooking; known for chicken couscous.

places.name: Caracoya
places.note: Hilltop dining room in the old city serving traditional couscous with a bay view.

places.name: Restaurant Timgad
places.note: Near the Botanical Garden; couscous and grilled fish in a traditional setting.

food.name: Chorba frik
food.desc: Tomato-based lamb soup thickened with freekeh, the green cracked wheat, and scented with mint and coriander. The staple opening course.

places.name: Restaurant El Djenina
places.note: Widely recommended for its hearty chorba and dolma at around 800 DZD a head.

places.name: Dar Dzair
places.note: Restored Ottoman house serving home-style Algerois cooking, chorba included.

places.name: Caracoya
places.note: Casbah kitchen doing the standard Algerian soup-then-couscous progression well.

food.name: Rechta
food.desc: Fine hand-cut steamed noodles under a pale cinnamon-scented chicken and turnip broth with chickpeas. The Algerois Friday and festival dish.

places.name: Dar Dzair
places.note: One of the few restaurants reliably cooking rechta the traditional Algerois way.

places.name: Restaurant El Djenina
places.note: Old-city dining room with rechta and other capital specialities on rotation.

places.name: Caracoya
places.note: Traditional menu that includes rechta alongside couscous when in season.

food.name: Garantita
food.desc: Baked chickpea-flour custard cut into thick slices, dusted with cumin and harissa and stuffed into a baguette. The great Algerian street snack.

places.name: Bab El Oued street carts
places.note: The city's best-known garantita carts, working from morning until late night.

places.name: Place des Martyrs carts
places.note: Stands near the ferry terminal and metro entrance; around 100 DZD a portion.

places.name: Rue Larbi Ben Mhidi snack counters
places.note: Downtown counters selling garantita and mhadjeb through the afternoon.

food.name: Mhadjeb
food.desc: Thin semolina crepes folded around a slow-cooked onion, tomato and pepper filling, then griddled flat. Sold folded in paper and eaten walking.

places.name: Bab El Oued street stalls
places.note: Griddled to order in front of you; the classic late-night Algiers snack.

places.name: Casbah market stalls
places.note: Small counters through the old city selling mhadjeb and mahjouba all day.

places.name: Rue Didouche Mourad snack bars
places.note: Downtown quick-eat counters on the main shopping street.

food.name: Makroud
food.desc: Semolina diamonds stuffed with cinnamon-spiced date paste, fried and dipped in honey. Sold from patisseries and late-night carts across the city.

places.name: Rue Didouche Mourad patisseries
places.note: French-influenced pastry shops that trade well past midnight.

places.name: Bab El Oued makroud carts
places.note: Late-night carts selling makroud alongside grilled corn and merguez rolls.

places.name: Casbah pastry shops
places.note: Old-city shops selling makroud, baklawa and samsa by weight.

food.name: Mint tea and cafe casse
food.desc: Sweet green tea with mint and pine nuts, or the Algerois cafe casse, a short espresso cut with a splash of hot milk. No alcohol needed.

places.name: Milk Bar Cafe
places.note: Historic downtown cafe, a landmark of the city with pastries and mint tea.

places.name: Cafe Tontonville
places.note: Long-established central cafe good for people-watching over tea or coffee.

places.name: Casbah terrace cafes
places.note: Rooftop and stepped-lane cafes serving mint tea above the bay.

food.name: Fresh citrus juice and citronnade
food.desc: Algeria's Mitidja oranges pressed to order, plus citronnade, a lemon-and-mint cooler, and sharbat almond milk drunk on feast days.

places.name: Marche Ali Mellah juice counters
places.note: Market juice bars pressing oranges and lemons through the morning.

places.name: Rue Didouche Mourad juice bars
places.note: Street-front counters on the main avenue serving orange and mixed juices.

places.name: Bab El Oued market stalls
places.note: Cheap fresh-squeezed juices next to the street-food carts.

landmarks: Notre-Dame d'Afrique
A Moorish-Byzantine basilica perched on a clifftop overlooking the Mediterranean, offering sweeping views of the bay.
Casbah of Algiers
A UNESCO World Heritage Ottoman-era citadel of winding alleys and whitewashed houses cascading down to the sea.
Maqam Echahid (Martyrs' Memorial)
A soaring 92-meter concrete monument shaped like three palm leaves, honoring Algeria's independence struggle and dominating the skyline.
Grande Poste d'Alger
A stunning neo-Moorish central post office from 1910, one of the most photographed pieces of colonial-era architecture in the city.
Djamaa el Djazair (Great Mosque of Algiers)
One of the world's largest mosques, featuring the tallest minaret on the planet and a striking modern silhouette over the bay.
Ketchaoua Mosque
A historic mosque at the edge of the Casbah blending Ottoman and Moorish styles, once converted into a cathedral and back again.
Bardo National Museum
A former 18th-century Ottoman palace housing prehistoric and ethnographic collections in an elegant courtyard setting.
Jardin d'Essai du Hamma
A lush 19th-century botanical garden famous for its palm-lined avenues that have appeared in Tarzan films.
Place des Martyrs
The historic heart of Algiers at the edge of the Casbah, framed by the harbor and bustling with daily life.
Bastion 23 / Palais des Raïs
A restored waterfront complex of Ottoman-era palaces once home to Algiers' corsair rulers, right on the Casbah's seafront.

train.note: No international trains run from Algiers itself. Algeria's only cross-border passenger train (to Tunis) departs from Annaba in the far east, and the Morocco border is closed to rail. Domestically, SNTF runs frequent day trains from Algiers-Agha to Oran, plus overnight sleeper trains with couchettes from Algiers to Constantine and to Annaba (departing around 21:30).

bus.note: A direct Algiers-Tunis coach (Tunisian operator SNTRI with Algeria's SOGRAL) launched in March 2026, leaving the SOGRAL bus station in Chéraga, west of Algiers, on Thursday and Saturday evenings; bring your passport. The Morocco land border is closed, so no coaches run west.

ferry.note: Car and passenger ferries to Europe leave from the Gare Maritime in central Algiers. Algérie Ferries (the national line, ENTMV) sails to Marseille and Alicante, and France's Corsica Linea also runs Marseille-Algiers. Schedules shift with the seasons and summer sailings sell out early, so book well ahead and carry a valid Schengen visa.
